chapter: Teddy Wilson, Cafe Society and bebop
title: Reaction to bebop and Parker and Dizzy
summary: Players feared they were finished, many trumpeters lost their minds, and Cheatham could not understand it then but now likes it.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: So when did you first realize that there was something called be-bop?
Well, after -- as soon as Charlie Parker and Dizzy got together. Then they started to -- recording that they made together. That's when I first realized that things were changing.
Uh-huh.

And everybody was getting upset about it because they thought if you couldn't play that then you're through. You couldn't play that type of jazz then you were through. That was the way everyone was feeling at that time.
So everything else was going to come to a stop.
Yeah, everything was going. And it looked like that was (what was) happening at that time.
Uh-huh.
So many trumpet players stopped and tried to play that style, lot of them just went crazy. Lost their minds.
Did you try it?
No. I couldn't -- I just couldn't find my way -- I couldn't see how to get into it.
Well you had already had to adapt to swing?
I had adapted to the New Orleans type of playing, --
Then you got into swing.
Got into swing, yeah.
And I was -- supposed this was of course a much bigger jump than going from New Orleans to swing?
Oh yes. I didn't see no way in the world that I could adopt to that because I didn't understand it.
Uh-huh.
I didn't understand it at all. I couldn't figure it out -- what was happening and I didn't like
it and it didn't make sense to me at the time.
So how does it sound to you now?
I like it.
You got used to it?
I listen to it all the time, I like it. Because you had, you see, Dizzy approved so much, because Dizzy was a good swing trumpeter in the beginning.
Yeah.
And that made a difference.
Uh-huh.

Made a big difference and you had other guys that came behind him, and that I liked too. And then it started making a lot of sense, because now Dizzy's making lot a sense, what he's playing now. I like it, I can understand it.
Well now it sounds almost traditional compared to some of the things --
That's right.
-- that are happening today.
That's right.
